{{Short description|Process during the early universe}}
{{Physical cosmology|expanded=early}}

In [[physical cosmology]], '''Big Bang nucleosynthesis''' (also known as '''primordial nucleosynthesis''', and abbreviated as '''BBN''')<ref name="RPP">{{cite journal |last=Patrignani |first=C. |date=2016 |title=Big-Bang nucleosynthesis |url=http://pdg.lbl.gov/2016/reviews/rpp2016-rev-bbang-nucleosynthesis.pdf |url-status=live |journal=Chin. Phys. C |volume=40 |page=100001 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161201063050/http://pdg.lbl.gov/2016/reviews/rpp2016-rev-bbang-nucleosynthesis.pdf |archive-date=2016-12-01 |collaboration=Particle Data Group}}</ref> is a model for the production of light [[Atomic nucleus|nuclei]] (including, but not limited to, [[Deuterium|<sup>2</sup>H]], <sup>3</sup>He, <sup>4</sup>He, and <sup>7</sup>Li) during the first ~20 minutes of the evolution of the [[universe]].<ref name=Schramm-1998>{{Cite journal |last1=Schramm |first1=David N. |last2=Turner |first2=Michael S. |date=1998-01-01 |title=Big-bang nucleosynthesis enters the precision era |url=https://journals.aps.org/rmp/abstract/10.1103/RevModPhys.70.303 |journal=Reviews of Modern Physics |volume=70 |issue=1 |pages=303–318 |doi=10.1103/RevModPhys.70.303|arxiv=astro-ph/9706069 |bibcode=1998RvMP...70..303S }}</ref> The predictions of BBN rely on a combination of thermodynamic arguments and measurements of rates of nuclear reactions that are expected to be active in the [[early universe]]. Refined models tend to agree well with observations of these light element abundances. The model is one of the key concepts in standard cosmology.

Elements heavier than lithium are instead created in appreciable amounts at later times via [[stellar nucleosynthesis]], through the formation, evolution and death of stars.

==History==

The history of Big Bang nucleosynthesis research began with [[George Gamow]], a nuclear physicist who thought that [[Victor Goldschmidt]]'s data on the [[abundance of elements]] in the universe might be predicted by nuclear reactions. Early in the 1940s Gamow realized that very high temperatures and pressures needed for nuclear reactions implied an explosion followed by expansion.<ref name=KarghCosmos>{{Cite book |last=Kragh |first=Helge |title=Conceptions of cosmos: from myths to the accelerating universe: a history of cosmology |date=2007 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-920916-3 |location=Oxford; New York}}</ref>{{rp|177}} Calculations by his student [[Ralph Alpher]], published<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Alpher|first1=R. A.|last2=Bethe|first2=H.|author-link2=Hans Bethe|last3=Gamow|first3=G.|author-link3=George Gamow|date=1 April 1948|title=The Origin of Chemical Elements|journal=[[Physical Review]]|volume=73|issue=7|pages=803–804|bibcode=1948PhRv...73..803A|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.73.803|pmid=18877094|author-link1=Ralph Asher Alpher|doi-access=free}}<!--|access-date=2011-03-10 --></ref> in the famous [[Alpher–Bethe–Gamow paper]], outlined an early theory of light-element production in the early universe. These early efforts did not involve specific nuclear reactions. When [[Enrico Fermi]] and [[Anthony L. Turkevich]] tried, they found they would predict hydrogen and helium, but no higher elements. The key problem was a "mass gap": there are no nuclei with masses of 5 and 8 atomic mass units needed for the reactions to reach higher masses. In 1953 this problem seemed insurmountable and cast doubt on the entire concept.<ref name=KarghCosmos/>{{rp|181}}

The competing cosmological model, the [[steady state model]], appearing in two 1948 publications by [[Fred Hoyle]] and by [[Herman Bondi]] and [[Thomas Gold]], had no mass-gap issue because it ignored nuclear processes initially. In 1957, Hoyle teamed up with [[Margaret Burbidge]], [[Geoffrey Burbidge]], [[William A. Fowler]] to develop a 
[[B2FH paper|detailed model of nucleosynthesis in stars]]. This theory matched the abundance of almost all of the elements except for hydrogen and helium, the elements correctly predicted by the Big Bang theory.<ref name=KarghCosmos/>{{rp|190}}

The discovery of the [[cosmic microwave background radiation]] in 1965 strongly supported the Big Bang theory and it also allowed [[Jim Peebles]] to use the estimated background temperature, 3K, in the first detailed calculations of the primordial isotopic abundances,<ref name="Primordial Helium">{{Cite journal | doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.16.410| title=Primeval Helium Abundance and the Primeval Fireball| journal=Physical Review Letters| volume=16| issue=10| pages=410–413| year=1966| last1=Peebles| first1=P. J. E.| bibcode=1966PhRvL..16..410P}}</ref> showing a He abundance between 26 and 28%. The following year Hoyle, Fowler, and Robert Wagoner showed that the very light elements like He require higher temperatures than stars provide,<ref name="Primordial Elements">Wagoner, Fowler and Hoyle [http://articles.adsabs.harvard.edu/cgi-bin/nph-iarticle_query?1967ApJ...148....3W&amp;data_type=PDF_HIGH&amp;whole_paper=YES&amp;type=PRINTER&amp;filetype=.pdf "ON THE SYNTHESIS OF ELEMENTS AT VERY HIGH TEMPERATURES"], ''Robert V. Wagoner, William A. Fowler, and F. Hoyle, The Astrophysical Journal, Vol. 148, April 1967.''</ref> evidence that most scientists took as support for the Big Bang model.<ref name=KarghCosmos/>{{rp|206}}

In 1972 the [[Copernicus satellite]] began to provide accurate measurements of [[deuterium]] abundance. Since primordial synthesis of deuterium depends more strongly on [[baryon]] density than does synthesis of <sup>3</sup>He, the deuterium abundance could be used to infer primordial density. By the 1990s additional measurements concluded that this density implied there must be mass other than baryons in the universe, an idea that came to be called [[dark matter]].<ref name=KarghCosmos/>{{rp|206}}  <ref>{{cite book |last=Schramm |first=D. N. |author-link=David Schramm (astrophysicist) |url=https://archive.org/details/bigbangotherexpl0000schr |title=The Big Bang and Other Explosions in Nuclear and Particle Astrophysics |publisher=World Scientific |year=1996 |isbn=978-981-02-2024-2 |location=Singapore |page=[https://archive.org/details/bigbangotherexpl0000schr/page/175 175] |url-access=registration}}</ref>

These nucleosynthesis methods have been refined over the years using updated estimates of the input nuclear reaction rates.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Hashimoto |first1=Masa-aki |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-981-13-2935-7 |title=Big-Bang Nucleosynthesis: Thermonuclear History in the Early Universe |last2=Nakamura |first2=Riou |last3=Thushari |first3=E. P. Berni Ann |last4=Arai |first4=Kenzo |date=2018 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-981-13-2935-7 |series=SpringerBriefs in Physics Ser |location=Singapore |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-981-13-2935-7 |issn=2191-5423}}</ref>{{rp|3}} The first systematic [[Monte Carlo integration|Monte Carlo]] study of how nuclear reaction rate uncertainties impact isotope predictions, over the relevant temperature range, was carried out in 1993.<ref name="Primordial Elements Monte Carlo">Smith, Kawano, and Malaney. [http://articles.adsabs.harvard.edu/cgi-bin/nph-iarticle_query?1993ApJS...85..219S&amp;data_type=PDF_HIGH&amp;whole_paper=YES&amp;type=PRINTER&amp;filetype=.pdf "EXPERIMENTAL, COMPUTATIONAL, AND OBSERVATIONAL ANALYSIS OF PRIMORDIAL NUCLEOSYNTHESIS"], ''Michael S. Smith, Lawrence H. Kawano and Robert A. Malaney, The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series, 85:219-247, 1993 April.''</ref>

==Physical description==
[[Image:Nuclear abundances.png|thumb|upright=1.4|The abundances of light element nuclei during Big Bang nucleosynthesis, as a function of time since the Big Bang in seconds (lower axis) or the [[Standard Model]] plasma temperature in [[MeV]].<ref name=PRIMAT>{{Cite journal |last1=Pitrou |first1=Cyril |last2=Coc |first2=Alain|last3=Uzan | first3=Jean-Phillipe| last4=Vangioni |first4 = Elisabeth |date=2018-09-03 |title=Precision big bang nucleosynthesis with improved Helium-4 predictions|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0370157318301054 |journal=Physics Reports |volume=754 |issue=1 |pages=1–66 |doi=10.1016/j.physrep.2018.04.005|arxiv=1801.08023 |bibcode=2018PhR...754....1P }}</ref>  The y-axis shows the abundance as a number density of each individual species divided by the number density of [[baryon]]s.]]
Big Bang nucleosynthesis describes the production of atomic nuclei from protons and neutrons in the expanding and cooling early universe. The process occurs at equilibrium with protons and neutrons combining to create nuclei and the nuclei disintegrating. As the temperature and pressure drop, equilibrium shifts to favor a few light element nuclei. Further expansion stops the BBN processes, setting the initial cosmic abundance of these elements.<ref name=Schramm-1991>{{Cite journal |last=Schramm |first=David N |date=January 1, 1991 |title=Big Bang nucleosynthesis: the Standard Model and alternatives |url=https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/0031-8949/1991/T36/003 |journal=Physica Scripta |volume=T36 |pages=22–29 |doi=10.1088/0031-8949/1991/T36/003 |bibcode=1991PhST...36...22S |issn=0031-8949 |url-access=subscription }} available in {{Cite book |last=Schramm |first=David N. |title=The big bang and other explosions in nuclear and particle astrophysics |date=1996 |publisher=World Scientific |isbn=978-981-02-2024-2 |location=Singapore| oclc=1147737739}}</ref>{{rp|36}}

The cosmic expansion process during BBN is described by the [[Friedmann–Robertson–Walker model]]. These equations completely determine the rate of expansion of the universe, as well as the evolution of the energy densities of different particle species.<ref name="Kolb-1990" /> In particular, these equations indicate that the universe becomes less dense and the temperature of particles in the [[Standard Model]] falls as BBN proceeds.

At temperatures above 1–2 [[Electronvolt|MeV]], [[proton]]s and [[neutron]]s interconverted via the [[weak interaction]]. As the temperature dropped, these reactions fell out of equilibrium, neutrons primarily decayed to protons, and the neutron-to-proton ratio fell to around 1/7.<ref name="Schramm-1998" />{{rp|315}} This sets the initial conditions for the onset of the formation of light nuclei.<ref name="Dodelson-2003" />{{rp|63}}

BBN began in earnest when the temperature of Standard Model particles dropped below roughly 1 MeV.<ref name="Kolb-1990">{{Cite book |last1=Kolb |first1=Edward W. |title=The early universe |last2=Turner |first2=Michael Stanley |date=1990 |publisher=Addison-Wesley |isbn=978-0-201-11603-8 |series=Frontiers in physics |location=Reading, Mass}}</ref> At this temperature, the average energy of [[photon]]s in the early universe was too low to break apart [[deuterium]] as it formed, but the universe remained hot and dense enough for [[Nuclear fusion|fusion]] reactions to occur at a significant rate.<ref name="RPP" />  This meant that a substantial population of deuterium formed.

This deuterium then fused to heavier nuclei, including [[tritium]], [[helium-3]], [[helium-4]], and [[lithium-7]].<ref name="Schramm-1998" />{{rp|315}} Helium-4 has a large [[Nuclear binding energy|binding energy]], which means that once a helium-4 nucleus is formed, it is difficult to break apart and incorporate its constituents into heavier nuclei. As a result of this, matter in the universe after BBN is primarily hydrogen and helium.<ref name="Dodelson-2003">{{Cite book |last=Dodelson |first=Scott |title=Modern cosmology |date=2003 |publisher=Academic Press |isbn=978-0-12-219141-1 |location=San Diego, Calif}}</ref>{{rp|68}} Standard BBN predicts, by the time BBN ends, the universe is composed of about 75% of hydrogen and 25% helium-4 by mass. Roughly 1 nucleus in 100,000 is deuterium or helium-3, and 1 nucleus in 1,000,000,000 is lithium-7. Even smaller amounts of heavier elements, as heavy as [[oxygen-20]], have been predicted to form.<ref name="PRIMAT" />

BBN coincides or nearly coincides with two other important events in cosmology. [[Neutrino decoupling]] occurred when the weak interaction fell out of equilibrium,<ref>{{cite journal |last=Dolgov |first=A. D. |title=Neutrinos in cosmology |journal=Physics Reports |date=2002-04-19 |volume=370 |issue=4–5 |pages=333–535 |doi=10.1016/S0370-1573(02)00139-4 |arxiv=hep-ph/0202122 |bibcode=2002PhR...370..333D }}</ref> just before BBN began. [[Electron–positron annihilation]] occurred during BBN, at around 0.5 MeV, when photons no longer had enough energy to convert back to [[electron]]s and [[positron]]s to maintain equilibrium.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Baumann |first=Daniel |title=Cosmology |date=2022 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-108-93709-2 |location=Cambridge, United Kingdom New York, NY}}</ref> This resulted in the depletion of the abundance of positrons in the universe, and heated photons. Since electron–positron annihilation occurred after neutrino decoupling, neutrinos did not heat alongside photons when electrons and positrons annihilated, and photons developed a separate temperature from neutrinos. This has important consequences for the rates of proton–neutron interconversion and the prediction of light element abundances.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Grohs |first1=E. |last2=Fuller |first2=George M. |date=2016-10-01 |title=The surprising influence of late charged current weak interactions on Big Bang Nucleosynthesis |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0550321316302644 |journal=Nuclear Physics B |volume=911 |pages=955–973 |doi=10.1016/j.nuclphysb.2016.08.034 |arxiv=1607.02797 |bibcode=2016NuPhB.911..955G |issn=0550-3213}}</ref>

==Determination of light element abundances==

=== Important parameters ===
The creation of light elements during BBN was dependent on nuclear reaction rate parameters and two cosmological input parameters neutron–proton ratio (calculable from [[Standard Model|Standard Model physics]]) and the baryon-photon ratio. The nuclear reaction rates are well-known from detailed laboratory studies at similar temperatures to those that appear in BBN.<ref name=Schramm-1991/>

==== Baryon-to-photon ratio ====
[[Image:Abundances vary baryon density.gif|thumb|upright=1.4|The evolution of different light element abundances for different values of the baryon-to-photon ratio η.<ref name=LINX>{{Cite journal |last1=Giovanetti |first1=Cara |last2=Lisanti |first2=Mariangela |last3=Liu | first3=Hongwan | last4=Mishra-Sharma |first4 = Siddharth | last5=Ruderman|first5=Joshua T.|date=2025-09-17 |title=Fast, differentiable, and extensible big bang nucleosynthesis package|url=https://journals.aps.org/prd/abstract/10.1103/f3tj-r882 |journal=Physical Review D |volume=112 |issue=6 |page=063531 |doi=10.1103/f3tj-r882|arxiv=2408.14538 |bibcode=2025PhRvD.112f3531G }}</ref> Note the final abundances (values at the latest times) can vary dramatically depending on the value of this parameter.]]

Light element abundances, and in particular deuterium, are sensitive to the value of the baryon-to-photon number ratio, η, which is the ratio of the [[number density]] of baryons to the number density of photons. Its value is small, at roughly 6 × 10<sup>−10</sup>.<ref name=":2">{{cite journal |last1=Collaboration |first1=Planck |title=''Planck'' 2018 results |date=2021-08-09 |arxiv=1807.06209 |last2=Aghanim |first2=N. |last3=Akrami |first3=Y. |last4=Ashdown |first4=M. |last5=Aumont |first5=J. |last6=Baccigalupi |first6=C. |last7=Ballardini |first7=M. |last8=Banday |first8=A. J. |last9=Barreiro |first9=R. B. |journal=Astronomy & Astrophysics |volume=641 |pages=A6 |doi=10.1051/0004-6361/201833910  |doi-access=free}}</ref> This parameter is proportional to the [[baryon]] density and controls the [[entropy]] of the universe, which in turn determines the temperature at which nuclear fusion can begin.<ref name="Kolb-1990" /> High entropy prevents light element nuclei from forming, which delays the onset of BBN; low entropy conversely lets BBN last longer, and therefore depletes the abundances of light elements that can fuse into helium-4.

Deuterium in particular is extremely sensitive to the value of the baryon-to-photon ratio;<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Olive |first1=Keith A |last2=Steigman |first2=Gary |last3=Walker |first3=Terry P |date=2000-08-01 |title=Primordial nucleosynthesis: theory and observations |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0370157300000314 |journal=Physics Reports |volume=333-334 |pages=389–407 |doi=10.1016/S0370-1573(00)00031-4 |arxiv=astro-ph/9905320 |bibcode=2000PhR...333..389O |issn=0370-1573}}</ref> decreasing η by a factor of 10 leads to a corresponding increase in the abundance of primordial deuterium by a factor of roughly 50.<ref name="RPP" />

==== Expansion rate ====
Particles and nuclei fall out of equilibrium when their rates of interaction become slower than the rate of the expansion of the universe. If the rate keeping a nuclear species in equilibrium drops below the expansion rate, the relative abundance of that species stops evolving (or decreases if decay is possible).<ref name="Longair-2008">{{cite book|last1=Longair|first1=M.S.|title=Galaxy formation|date=2008|publisher=Springer|location=Berlin|edition=2nd|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=e-wJHSBOuZAC&q=longair+neutrino+decoupling&pg=PA290|isbn=978-3-540-73477-2}}</ref>{{rp|340}}

During BBN, the universe is [[Scale factor (cosmology)#Radiation-dominated era|radiation dominated]], and so the expansion of the universe is primarily determined by the energy density in radiative species like photons and neutrinos. Light element abundances are therefore sensitive to the energy densities of these species.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mangano |first1=Gianpiero |title=A robust upper limit on <math>Neff</math> from BBN, circa 2011 |date=2011-06-10 |arxiv=1103.1261 |last2=Serpico |first2=Pasquale D. |journal=Physics Letters B |volume=701 |issue=3 |pages=296–299 |doi=10.1016/j.physletb.2011.05.075 }}</ref>

=== Sequence of nucleosynthesis ===
[[File:Main nuclear reaction chains for Big Bang nucleosynthesis.svg|right|thumb|upright=1.4|Main nuclear reaction chains for Big Bang nucleosynthesis]]
BBN begins shortly after neutrinos decouple from the Standard Model and processes interconverting protons and neutrons fall out of equilibrium.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |title=Big Bang Nucleosynthesis: Probing the First 20 Minutes - G. Steigman |url=https://ned.ipac.caltech.edu/level5/March04/Steigman/frames.html |access-date=2026-08-31 |website=ned.ipac.caltech.edu}}</ref> By roughly 20 seconds after the Big Bang, the universe had cooled sufficiently to allow deuterium nuclei to survive disruption by high-energy photons. At this time, there were about six protons for every neutron.

As the universe expanded and cooled, other light elements began to form, becoming heavier through nuclear fusion. At temperatures below 0.3 MeV, conditions were right for helium-4 to form, and below 0.1 MeV the abundance of deuterium climbed high enough for a burst of element formation.<ref name="Kolb-1990" /> However, very shortly thereafter, around twenty minutes after the Big Bang, the temperature and density became too low for any significant fusion to occur. At this point, the elemental abundances were nearly fixed. Further changes were the result of the [[radioactive]] decay of the two major unstable products of BBN, [[tritium]] and [[beryllium-7]],<ref>{{cite web |last=Weiss |first=Achim |title=Equilibrium and change: The physics behind Big Bang Nucleosynthesis |url=http://www.einstein-online.info/en/spotlights/BBN_phys/index.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070208212219/http://www.einstein-online.info/en/spotlights/BBN_phys/index.html |archive-date=8 February 2007 |access-date=2007-02-24 |website=Einstein Online}}</ref>  as well as continued decay of neutrons that did not fuse into any nuclei. At the end of nucleosynthesis there were about seven protons to every neutron, and almost all the neutrons were in Helium-4 nuclei.<ref>{{cite book |last=Bertulani |first=Carlos A. |author-link=Carlos Bertulani |title=Nuclei in the Cosmos |date=2013 |publisher=World Scientific |isbn=978-981-4417-66-2}}</ref>

==== Neutron–proton interconversion ====
At temperatures above roughly 2 MeV (roughly 1 second to 1 minute after the Big Bang), protons and neutrons interconverted via reactions involving electrons, positrons, neutrinos, and antineutrinos:<ref name=":5" />
:<chem>n \ + e+ <=> \overline{\nu}_e + p  </chem>
:<chem>n \ + \nu_{e} <=> p + e- </chem>

At times much earlier than 1 second, these reactions were fast and maintained a neutron/proton ratio close to 1. Neutrons are slightly heavier than protons, so even though these rates remained in equilibrium as the temperature began to drop, equilibrium shifted in favor of protons and the neutron/proton ratio smoothly decreased. Around a temperature of 2 MeV, these reactions fell out of equilibrium as neutrinos decoupled from the rest of the Standard Model. After this time, interconversion between protons and neutrons became inefficient, and the neutron-proton ratio was fixed to about 1/6.<ref name="Kolb-1990" />

However, this fraction continued to evolve during BBN, since [[free neutron]]s are unstable with a lifetime of about 15 minutes.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wietfeldt |first1=Fred E. |last2=Greene |first2=Geoffrey L. |date=2011-11-03 |title=Colloquium: The neutron lifetime |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/RevModPhys.83.1173 |journal=Reviews of Modern Physics |language=en |volume=83 |issue=4 |pages=1173–1192 |doi=10.1103/RevModPhys.83.1173 |bibcode=2011RvMP...83.1173W |issn=0034-6861|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Had nucleosynthesis not occurred, this ratio would have fallen to 0, but since neutrons are usually stable when bound in nuclei, the neutron/proton ratio settles to about 1/7 by the end of BBN.<ref name="Kolb-1990" /> Virtually all of these remaining neutrons are therefore incorporated into nuclei at the end of BBN.

==== Deuterium ====
Deuterium is the first nucleus to fuse during BBN. Its formation is the first step in all reaction chains to synthesize heavier elements. It has a small [[Nuclear binding energy|binding energy]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Van Der Leun |first1=C. |last2=Alderliesten |first2=C. |date=1982-05-24 |title=The deuteron binding energy |journal=Nuclear Physics A |volume=380 |issue=2 |pages=261–269 |doi=10.1016/0375-9474(82)90105-1 |bibcode=1982NuPhA.380..261V |issn=0375-9474}}</ref> meaning it is generally easy to break deuterium nuclei apart and incorporate them into heavier nuclei. For example, to fuse tritium, a deuterium nucleus breaks when it encounters another deuterium nucleus, and the neutron from the first nucleus is incorporated into the second. This process is efficient because the deuterium binding energy is low.

The deuterium abundance climbs steadily during BBN until temperatures lower than about 0.1 MeV.<ref name="PRIMAT" /> After that, deuterium fusion becomes inefficient due to the decreasing temperature and density of the universe. BBN proceeds for a time as the remaining deuterium is fused into heavier nuclei, but eventually those processes become inefficient as well and a tiny abundance of deuterium (roughly one out of every 100,000 nuclei) remains.

==== Tritium, helium-3, and helium-4 ====
Tritium and helium-3 form next, when the deuterium abundance is large enough that deuterium fuses efficiently. Helium-4 forms quickly thereafter, reaching an appreciable abundance roughly 10 seconds after the Big Bang, and quickly surpassing the deuterium abundance thereafter as deuterium is consumed to make heavier elements.<ref name=":0" /> Helium-4 has a very large binding energy compared to all other nuclei of similar atomic weight.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Audi |first1=G. |last2=Wapstra |first2=A. H. |date=1995-12-25 |title=The 1995 update to the atomic mass evaluation |journal=Nuclear Physics A |volume=595 |issue=4 |pages=409–480 |doi=10.1016/0375-9474(95)00445-9 |bibcode=1995NuPhA.595..409A |issn=0375-9474}}</ref> Unlike deuterium, processes that require fusing helium-4 nuclei with other nuclei are therefore inefficient. Further, the absence of a stable nucleus with 5 or 8 nucleons means it is impossible to fuse helium-4 with helium-4, or helium-4 with protons, the two most abundant nuclei in the universe.

The helium-4 abundance closely tracks the neutron abundance. Neutrons that did not decay during BBN are very likely to be in a helium-4 nucleus, since helium-4 must be formed on the way to heavier elements and incorporating additional nucleons requires significant energy. The neutron/proton ratio alone is sufficient to estimate that about 8% of all atoms should be helium-4, leading to a mass fraction of helium-4 of about 25%. This estimate is in accordance with observations.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal |author=Gary Steigman |year=2007 |title=Primordial Nucleosynthesis in the Precision Cosmology Era |journal=[[Annual Review of Nuclear and Particle Science]] |volume=57 |issue=1 |pages=463–491 |arxiv=0712.1100 |bibcode=2007ARNPS..57..463S |doi=10.1146/annurev.nucl.56.080805.140437 |s2cid=118473571 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

==== Heavier elements ====
{{Nucleosynthesis periodic table.svg}}
Trace amounts of elements heavier than helium-4 also form during BBN. These abundances are suppressed tightly&mdash;bound helium-4 must be produced and then broken apart in order to form heavier nuclei. Elements heavier than helium-4 are instead primarily produced in [[stellar nucleosynthesis|stars]], where this bottleneck is overcome via triple collisions of helium-4 nuclei, producing [[carbon]] (the [[triple-alpha process]]).<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sølund Kirsebom |first=Oliver |date=2013 |title=12C and the triple-α reaction rate |url=https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1742-6596/436/1/012072 |journal=Journal of Physics: Conference Series |volume=436 |issue=12072 |article-number=012072 |doi=10.1088/1742-6596/436/1/012072 |via=IOPScience|doi-access=free }}</ref> This process is too slow to be relevant during BBN's 20-minute duration.

Precise numerical codes make predictions for the abundances of heavy elements as heavy as oxygen.<ref name="PRIMAT" /> These form sequentially during BBN, in reactions involving lighter nuclei that formed prior.

=== Measurements of primordial abundances ===
In order to test the predictions of BBN, astrophysicists make precise measurements of light element abundances in the universe. These measurements are complicated by the fact that stars change the relative abundances of hydrogen, deuterium, helium-3, helium-4, and heavier elements as the universe evolves. Therefore, measurements of primordial element abundances are taken in [[metal-poor]] systems, where contamination from [[stellar nucleosynthesis]] is expected to be low.<ref name=":5" />

Measurements of primordial deuterium involve measuring [[Absorption spectroscopy|absorption spectra]] from metal-poor clouds of gas passing in front of bright, distant [[quasar]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Cooke |first1=Ryan |title=One Percent Determination of the Primordial Deuterium Abundance |date=2018-03-26 |arxiv=1710.11129 |last2=Pettini |first2=Max |last3=Steidel |first3=Charles C. |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |volume=855 |issue=2 |page=102 |doi=10.3847/1538-4357/aaab53 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2018ApJ...855..102C }}</ref> Measurements of primordial helium-4 involve measuring helium-4 recombination lines, emitted when an electron and ionized helium-4 combine back into a neutral atom, in metal-poor [[Dwarf galaxy|dwarf galaxies]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Aver |first1=Erik |title=The primordial helium abundance from updated emissivities |date=2013-08-30 |arxiv=1309.0047 |last2=Olive |first2=Keith A. |last3=Porter |first3=R. L. |last4=Skillman |first4=Evan D. |journal=Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics |issue=11 |page=017 |doi=10.1088/1475-7516/2013/11/017 |bibcode=2013JCAP...11..017A }}</ref> These two isotopes have each been measured to percent-level precision. The observed abundance of each of these nuclei is generally consistent with the abundances predicted by BBN.<ref name="Dodelson-2003" />{{rp|69}}<ref name="Schramm-1998" />{{rp|313}}

There are also measurements of primordial lithium-7, both in stars and in the [[interstellar medium]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Molaro |first1=P. |title=Extragalactic <sup>85</sup>Rb/<sup>87</sup>Rb and <sup>6</sup>Li/<sup>7</sup>Li ratios in the Small Magellanic Cloud |date=2024-07-15 |arxiv=2407.10818 |last2=Bonifacio |first2=P. |last3=Cupani |first3=G. |last4=Howk |first4=C. |journal=Astronomy & Astrophysics |volume=690 |pages=A38 |doi=10.1051/0004-6361/202449529  |doi-access=free|bibcode=2024A&A...690A..38M }}</ref> In the 1980s, measurements of [[Population II stars|Population II]] [[dwarf star]]s appeared to have similar abundances of lithium, despite having different metallicities.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Spite |first1=F. |last2=Spite |first2=M. |year=1982 |title=Abundance of lithium in unevolved stars and old disk stars: Interpretation and consequences. |url=https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1982A&A...115..357S/abstract |journal=Astronomy and Astrophysics |language=en |volume=115 |pages=357–366 |bibcode=1982A&A...115..357S |issn=0004-6361}}</ref> This result, called the [[Spite plateau]], was thought to coincide with the primordial lithium-7 abundance. However, more recent measurements of lower-metallicity stars have found a smaller lithium abundance, raising questions about the assumption that the abundance of lithium-7 on the Spite plateau is primordial.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sbordone |first1=L. |title=The metal-poor end of the Spite plateau |date=2010-08-17 |arxiv=1003.4510 |last2=Bonifacio |first2=P. |last3=Caffau |first3=E. |last4=Ludwig |first4=H.-G. |last5=Behara |first5=N. T. |last6=Hernandez |first6=J. I. Gonzalez |last7=Steffen |first7=M. |last8=Cayrel |first8=R. |last9=Freytag |first9=B. |journal=Astronomy & Astrophysics |volume=522 |pages=A26 |doi=10.1051/0004-6361/200913282  |doi-access=free}}</ref> The resulting measurement of primordial lithium-7 is a factor of 2'''–'''4 lower than the predicted BBN abundance,<ref>{{cite journal |author=R. H. Cyburt, B. D. Fields & K. A. Olive |year=2008 |title=A Bitter Pill: The Primordial Lithium Problem Worsens |journal=Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics |volume=2008 |issue=11 |page=012 |arxiv=0808.2818 |bibcode=2008JCAP...11..012C |doi=10.1088/1475-7516/2008/11/012 |s2cid=122212670}}</ref> a discrepancy known as the [[cosmological lithium problem]], though there remain open questions about the Spite plateau and the reliability of these measurements.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=E. X. |title=Non-detection of 6Li in Spite plateau stars with ESPRESSO |date=2021-10-11 |arxiv=2110.03822 |last2=Nordlander |first2=T. |last3=Asplund |first3=M. |last4=Lind |first4=K. |last5=Zhou |first5=Y. |last6=Reggiani |first6=H. |journal=Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society |volume=509 |pages=1521–1535 |doi=10.1093/mnras/stab2924 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Fields |first1=Brian D. |last2=Molaro |first2=Paolo |last3=Sarkar |first3=Subir |date=August 2023 |title=Reviews of Particle Physics. Chapter 24: Big Bang Nucleosynthesis |url=https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-bbang-nucleosynthesis.pdf |journal=Particle Data Group}}</ref>

Finally, there is an observational upper bound on the abundance of primordial helium-3. Primordial helium-3 is difficult to measure because systems are easily contaminated by nearby stellar activity, and measurements can vary widely with no clear correlation to metallicity or location of the system being measured.<ref name=":0" /> Therefore only an upper bound can be reported from observation (as contamination should increase the amount of helium-3 in the system),<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bania |first1=T. M. |last2=Rood |first2=Robert T. |last3=Balser |first3=Dana S. |year=2002 |title=The cosmological density of baryons from observations of 3He+ in the Milky Way |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/415054a |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=415 |issue=6867 |pages=54–57 |doi=10.1038/415054a |pmid=11780112 |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref> though it is not often used in precision analyses.<ref name=":1" />

==Significance==

=== For standard cosmology ===
BBN provides a direct measurement of the baryon-to-photon ratio, one of the six parameters in the [[Lambda-CDM model]] of cosmology.<ref name=":1" /> Deuterium in particular is extraordinarily sensitive to the value of this parameter; the baryon-to-photon ratio is determined by calculating the value of η that produces a prediction of the deuterium abundance that matches the measured abundance. Recent work uses BBN to determine the baryon-to-photon ratio with an uncertainty of 1%.<ref name=":4">{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jskjFvUQapc |title=2025 Gruber Cosmology Prize |date=2025-10-08 |last=The Gruber Foundation |access-date=2026-01-25 |via=YouTube}}</ref>

The baryon-to-photon ratio can also be inferred from the [[cosmic microwave background]] (CMB).<ref name=":2" /> BBN and the formation of the CMB are separated by roughly 400,000 years of evolution; they are two independent epochs in cosmology, and yet the Lambda-CDM model of cosmology requires they share the same value of the baryon-to-photon ratio. Concordance between these epochs is observed, and so Lambda-CDM passes this consistency test.<ref name=":4" />

Fitting the six parameters of Lambda-CDM to observed data from CMB experiments also requires knowledge of the primordial helium-4 abundance. While in some analyses this parameter is inferred from CMB data, state-of-the-art inference of the parameters of Lambda-CDM requires input from BBN.<ref name=":2" />

The BBN determination of the baryon-to-photon ratio is also used in analyses of [[Baryon acoustic oscillations|baryon acoustic oscillation]] (BAO) data. BAO is sensitive to the baryon-to-photon ratio, and in so in analyses where independence from the CMB is desired, the BBN determination of this parameter is used during data analysis.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Collaboration |first1=DESI |title=DESI 2024 VI: Cosmological constraints from the measurements of baryon acoustic oscillations |date=2025 |arxiv=2404.03002 |last2=Adame |first2=A. G. |last3=Aguilar |first3=J. |last4=Ahlen |first4=S. |last5=Alam |first5=S. |last6=Alexander |first6=D. M. |last7=Alvarez |first7=M. |last8=Alves |first8=O. |last9=Anand |first9=A. |journal=Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics |issue=2 |page=021 |doi=10.1088/1475-7516/2025/02/021 |bibcode=2025JCAP...02..021A }}</ref>

=== For new physics ===
BBN is often used to constrain particle physics scenarios beyond the Standard Model, including [[dark matter]] scenarios, massive [[neutrino]]s,<ref>Soler, F. J. P., Froggatt, C. D., & Muheim, F., eds., ''Neutrinos in Particle Physics, Astrophysics and Cosmology'' ([[Baton Rouge, Louisiana|Baton Rouge]]: [[CRC Press]], 2009), [https://books.google.com/books?id=mRGThuuYHgsC&pg=PA362 p. 362].</ref><ref>Anderson, R. W., ''The Cosmic Compendium: The Big Bang & the Early Universe'' ([[Morrisville, North Carolina|Morrisville, NC]]: [[Lulu (company)|Lulu Press, Inc.]], 2015), [https://books.google.com/books?id=9U6yCQAAQBAJ&pg=PA54 p. 54].</ref> and other particles or phenomena not included in the Standard Model.<ref name=":3">{{cite journal |last1=Pospelov |first1=Maxim |title=Big Bang Nucleosynthesis as a Probe of New Physics |date=2010-11-04 |arxiv=1011.1054 |last2=Pradler |first2=Josef |journal=Annual Review of Nuclear and Particle Science |volume=60 |pages=539–568 |doi=10.1146/annurev.nucl.012809.104521 |bibcode=2010ARNPS..60..539P }}</ref>

BBN takes place near temperatures of 1 MeV, and therefore is sensitive to processes that are characterized by a similar energy scale. In standard cosmology, this includes neutrino decoupling and electron–positron annihilation. Scenarios that include, for example, energy injections from exotic particles into the Standard Model plasma around the same temperature, can also be probed with BBN, as these new processes change the predictions for primordial element abundances.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Nollett |first1=Kenneth M. |title=BBN and the CMB constrain light, electromagnetically coupled WIMPs |date=2014-04-04 |arxiv=1312.5725 |last2=Steigman |first2=Gary |journal=Physical Review D |volume=89 |issue=8 |article-number=083508 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.89.083508 |bibcode=2014PhRvD..89h3508N }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Nollett |first1=Kenneth M. |title=BBN and the CMB constrain neutrino coupled light WIMPs |date=2015-02-12 |arxiv=1411.6005 |last2=Steigman |first2=Gary |journal=Physical Review D |volume=91 |issue=8 |article-number=083505 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.91.083505 |bibcode=2015PhRvD..91h3505N }}</ref> Other scenarios, including time-varying [[fundamental constants]] or scenarios with new light particles, can be probed in much the same way.<ref name=":3" />
